title: Logical Guidance of Stochastic Interpolants

paper.title: Logical Guidance of Stochastic Interpolants
paper.abstract:
Abstract Guidance and composition of generative models have applications in visual design, chemistry, and biology.
Logical guidance composes conditional scores exactly for diffusion models.
However, fm ( fm ) and si ( si ) learn velocity fields.
We show that negation and exclusive disjunction admit exact conditional velocity composition on any interpolant, whereas conjunction, and therefore any formula containing one, is exact on Gaussian paths but in general incurs a drift-interaction error, so composed velocities need not sample the logical target. LoGSI solves this by using score-based re-equilibration as our principled mechanism and falling back to the Gaussian-path velocity rule as an approximate transport predictor.
In non-Gaussian bridge problems, generation alternates transport steps with score re-equilibration steps.
On image transfer (EMNIST to CMNIST, CelebA) and QM9 source-to-target molecular editing with logical attribute constraints, LoGSI improves rule conformity at the same network-evaluation budget over composed-velocity baselines, while also improving fidelity on the image tasks.
More broadly, LoGSI applies wherever stochastic interpolants need guidance and logical combinations of constraints are natural.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Guidance and composition are central to generative AI, enabling controlled generation across domains ranging from visual design to chemistry and biology ( Saharia et al., 2022 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ; Watson et al., 2023 ; Skreta et al., 2025 ; Blohm and Garg, 2026 ) . Guidance steers a model toward desired properties, while composition combines multiple conditions or concepts to produce outputs that satisfy more complex requirements. Most existing methods target diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Song et al., 2020 ) , where one endpoint is a fixed Gaussian, and the reverse dynamics depend only on the score. A natural extension is to lift logical guidance to stochastic interpolants (SI) ( Albergo et al., 2025 ) , which unify diffusion and flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) and are not tied to a Gaussian endpoint. Classical guidance ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) for SI has been studied ( Feng et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) , but logical composition of atomic conditions in this regime remains open. We focus on domain transfer ( Liu et al., 2023 ) : an interpolant transports a source distribution ρ 0 \rho_{0} to a target ρ 1 \rho_{1} , samples can be initialized from concrete source instances ( Albergo et al., 2024 ) , and guidance enforces a Boolean formula φ \varphi over target attributes. For example, we may edit a source molecule by adding a geometry (e.g. rings) and an atom-composition constraint (e.g. oxygen). Throughout, we distinguish between unconditional velocity and score fields (or velocities and scores for short), denoted by v t ​ ( x ) v_{t}(x) and s t ​ ( x ) s_{t}(x) , and conditional velocity and score fields, denoted by v t ​ ( x ∣ c ) v_{t}(x\mid c) and s t ​ ( x ∣ c ) s_{t}(x\mid c) , which steer generation toward samples satisfying a constraint or property c c . The core challenge is that SIs learn conditional velocities, but it is not clear a priori how these fields should be combined to enforce a Boolean formula φ \varphi . For conditional scores, Alesiani et al. (2026) (LogDiff) derive exact recursive composition rules. We show that the analogous velocity composition is exact for Gaussian-path bridges, and that outside that regime it fails if the Boolean formula contains conjunctions or conditional-independent disjunctions (CI-disjunctions). We introduce LoGSI to address this asymmetry between velocity and score compositionality ( Figure 1 ). On general stochastic interpolants with a non-Gaussian starting distribution, both velocity and score are available at sampling time, but only the score admits exact logical composition for every formula ( Alesiani et al., 2026 ) . In LoGSI , composed velocities are exact on Gaussian-path bridges and can be used as a proxy transport field elsewhere. LoGSI therefore separates roles: an approximate transport step along the proxy transport field v ~ t ( ⋅ ∣ φ ) \tilde{v}_{t}(\cdot\mid\varphi) advances mass along the interpolant, while exact composed conditional scores re-equilibrate samples toward p t ( ⋅ ∣ φ ) p_{t}(\cdot\mid\varphi) at each timestep. In the limit of sufficient score-correction steps at fixed t t , the procedure is consistent with the logical target. Concretely, we realize this split as a transport–re-equilibration sampler: each outer step applies a transport update along v ~ t \tilde{v}_{t} , followed by K K overdamped Langevin steps with the exactly composed conditional score. We evaluate our method on image and molecular transfer with non-Gaussian endpoints, testing general Boolean templates (conjunction, disjunction, negation) and randomly generated expression trees. At matched network-evaluation budget, score-guided re-equilibration with a proxy velocity improves rule conformity over composed-velocity integration. It also yields higher fidelity on the image experiments. Figure 1: Overview of LoGSI . (a) Logical composition targets samples from ρ 1 \rho_{1} satisfying c 1 ∧ c 2 c_{1}\land c_{2} , transported from ρ 0 \rho_{0} by a stochastic interpolant, sampling can only use the atomic conditioned scores and velocities. (b) Scores compose exactly for general stochastic interpolants, velocity composition matches the same rule on Gaussian-path / diffusion bridges, except at negation and exclusive-disjunction nodes, which match on any interpolant ( Theorem 1 ). (c) Our method transports samples with a proxy velocity roughly pointing in the right direction, then re-equilibrates with the exactly composed conditional score. Our main contributions are as follows: • Score–velocity asymmetry for logical SI. On Gaussian-path flow matching, LogDiff score composition induces an exact velocity composition rule. For general stochastic interpolants with non-Gaussian endpoints, score composition carries over unchanged, velocity rules fail for conjunction and CI-disjunction, and therefore for general logical statements φ \varphi . • Logical guidance by score correction. We sample under Boolean formulas by re-equilibrating with exactly composed conditional scores at each timestep, avoiding any closed-form composed velocity field. • Proxy velocity transport. We reuse the Gaussian-path velocity rule as a transport proxy, cutting the number of correction steps needed and improving conformity over the composed-velocity baseline.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Generative methods and bridges. Diffusion models generate data by reversing a fixed noising process ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song and Ermon, 2020 ) , unified by Song et al. (2021) in the notion of stochastic processes. Song et al. (2021) also propose to sample with a predictor-corrector scheme, where a Langevin corrector uses the score to remove the predictor’s discretization error while both target the same marginal. Our sampler is similar but structurally different: because only the score composes exactly for formulas containing conjunctions or general disjunctions ( Remark 1 ), the score–velocity asymmetry ( Section 4.2 ) forces the transport step to be a deliberate proxy v ~ t ≠ v t ( ⋅ ∣ φ ) \tilde{v}_{t}\neq v_{t}(\cdot\mid\varphi) , while the corrector is the exactness mechanism enforcing the logical constraint, needed beyond discretization error even with infinitesimal transport steps. Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) learns a velocity field between two distributions, and stochastic interpolants ( Albergo et al., 2025 ) generalize both diffusion and flow matching while dropping the Gaussian-endpoint assumption, which is why we adopt them for our method. Finally, Schrödinger bridges ( De Bortoli et al., 2021 ; Shi et al., 2023 ) transport between arbitrary distributions under an entropy-optimal-transport objective. Since our logical composition is orthogonal to how the bridge is trained, extending it to such samplers is an appealing direction for future work. Guidance and compositional conditioning. Guidance of generative models was first achieved by training a separate classifier to steer diffusion sampling ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) . The noise-aware classifiers we use for the posterior weights in our logical composition play an analogous role. Classifier-free guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) shortly after removed the need for a separately trained classifier by jointly modeling conditional and unconditional scores. Both approaches condition on a single condition and do not address how multiple conditions should be combined. Compositional generation, started in products of experts ( Hinton, 2002 ) and revived more recently ( Du et al., 2023 ; Gaudi et al., 2025 ) , targets exactly this problem, and subsequent work developed compositional and logical conditioning for diffusion models ( Liu et al., 2022 ) . Closely related, Skreta et al. (2025) introduce SuperDiff, which composes pretrained diffusion models at inference time through logical AND and OR operators. We discuss the connection to our bridge setting in Section A.6 . Most relevant to us, Alesiani et al. (2026) derive exact recursive rules for composing conditional scores under Boolean formulas. Guidance has also been extended to flow matching ( Feng et al., 2025 ) and stochastic interpolants ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , but to our knowledge logical composition in these settings remains unexplored.

sections.text: We first characterize when logical composition extends from scores to velocities ( Section 4.1 ), identify exactly where this extension fails for general stochastic interpolants ( Section 4.2 ), and then describe our sampling method ( Sections 4.3 and 4.4 ) which resolves the problems.

sections.heading: 4.4 Proxy velocity for transport
sections.text: A natural, easy to compute transport step uses the unconditional velocity, v ~ t ​ ( x ∣ φ ) := v t ​ ( x ) \tilde{v}_{t}(x\mid\varphi):=v_{t}(x) . However, this step advances the sample along trajectories that are typically misaligned with p t ( ⋅ ∣ φ ) p_{t}(\cdot\mid\varphi) , therefore requiring many Langevin equilibration steps to re-equilibrate with the logical marginal at each noise level. We instead propose to use the Gaussian-path composition rule Equation 11 as a proxy velocity v ~ t ​ ( x ∣ φ ) = v ˇ t ​ ( x ∣ φ ) \tilde{v}_{t}(x\mid\varphi)=\check{v}_{t}(x\mid\varphi) , evaluated with the atomic conditional velocities of the trained stochastic interpolant. Outside the Gaussian-path regime this field is not equal to the true conditional velocity v t ​ ( x ∣ φ ) v_{t}(x\mid\varphi) in general ( Theorem 2 ), but it is the unique velocity that would be correct if the affine relation of Lemma 1 held. Additionally, by Theorem 1 it is exact at every negation and exclusive-disjunction node of φ \varphi , which is what makes Equation 11 a good transport field despite not being the conditional velocity in general. Empirically it reduces the burden on the corrector as shown in the experiment section.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied logical composition for stochastic interpolants that transport between non-Gaussian source and target distributions. While conditional scores compose exactly in the LogDiff sense on general interpolants, the analogous velocity rule survives only in part: negation and exclusive disjunction remain exact on any interpolant, whereas conjunction, and hence any formula containing one, is exact only on Gaussian-path bridges. LoGSI therefore separates roles: a proxy composed velocity advances samples along the interpolant, and exactly composed conditional scores re-equilibrate them toward p t ( ⋅ ∣ φ ) p_{t}(\cdot\mid\varphi) at each timestep. Across EMNIST-to-CMNIST, CelebA, and QM9 editing benchmarks, this transport–re-equilibration procedure improves logical conformity at matched network-evaluation budget over composed-velocity baselines, for both fixed Boolean templates and randomly generated formulas. It additionally improves fidelity (FID) on the image benchmarks and novelty on QM9. More broadly, the same score-based viewpoint may extend to other bridge learners and to settings where logical combinations of constraints arise together with non-Gaussian transport.

(2025) introduce a method to track changes in the conditional densities p t ​ ( x ∣ c i ) p_{t}(x\mid c_{i}) along a sample path without training a noise-aware classifier. Their Theorem 1 gives an Itô estimator for d ​ log ⁡ p t ​ ( x ∣ c i ) \mathrm{d}\log p_{t}(x\mid c_{i}) . In principle, this construction could also be applied to stochastic interpolants and bridges as in our setting, although they only develop it for diffusion models. For logical AND , they choose weights κ i \kappa_{i} (with ∑ i κ i = 1 \sum_{i}\kappa_{i}=1 ) by requiring equal infinitesimal density updates, d ​ log ⁡ p t ​ ( x ∣ c i ) = d ​ log ⁡ p t ​ ( x ∣ c j ) \mathrm{d}\log p_{t}(x\mid c_{i})=\mathrm{d}\log p_{t}(x\mid c_{j}) , and transport the state with a κ \kappa -weighted linear combination of the atomic SDE drifts, so that in expectation the endpoint is equally likely under each conditional model, p 1 ​ ( x ∣ c i ) = p 1 ​ ( x ∣ c j ) p_{1}(x\mid c_{i})=p_{1}(x\mid c_{j}) for all i , j i,j . Crucially, matching the increments d ​ log ⁡ p t ​ ( x ∣ c i ) \mathrm{d}\log p_{t}(x\mid c_{i}) along the trajectory only pins down terminal densities up to the initial gap : integrating from 0 0 to 1 1 gives log ⁡ p 1 ​ ( x 1 ∣ c i ) − log ⁡ p 1 ​ ( x 1 ∣ c j ) = log ⁡ p 0 ​ ( x 0 ∣ c i ) − log ⁡ p 0 ​ ( x 0 ∣ c j ) , \displaystyle\log p_{1}(x_{1}\mid c_{i})-\log p_{1}(x_{1}\mid c_{j})\;=\;\log p_{0}(x_{0}\mid c_{i})-\log p_{0}(x_{0}\mid c_{j}), (68) so the construction lands on the AND manifold { x : p 1 ( x ∣ c i ) = p 1 ( x ∣ c j ) ∀ i , j } \{x:p_{1}(x\mid c_{i})=p_{1}(x\mid c_{j})\ \forall i,j\} only when the initial laws already agree, p 0 ​ ( x ∣ c i ) = p 0 ​ ( x ∣ c j ) p_{0}(x\mid c_{i})=p_{0}(x\mid c_{j}) for all i , j i,j . This is true for standard diffusion models, where generation begins from a shared Gaussian independent of the condition, but fails in our bridge setting: we do not start from noise but from explicit samples x 0 ∼ ρ 0 x_{0}\sim\rho_{0} , and in general p 0 ​ ( x ∣ c i ) ≠ p 0 ​ ( x ∣ c j ) p_{0}(x\mid c_{i})\neq p_{0}(x\mid c_{j}) . By equation 68 , the endpoint gap then equals the initial gap and the resulting sample is not on the AND manifold. A further practical difference concerns the divergence term in their density update. For VP/OU diffusion, ⟨ ∇ , f t ⟩ \langle\nabla,f_{t}\rangle in Theorem 1 is available in closed form because the forward drift f t f_{t} is linear. For general stochastic interpolants one would instead need div \operatorname{div} of each atomic drift v t ( ⋅ ∣ c i ) + 1 2 γ ¯ ( t ) s t ( ⋅ ∣ c i ) v_{t}(\cdot\mid c_{i})+\tfrac{1}{2}\bar{\gamma}(t)\,s_{t}(\cdot\mid c_{i}) , which for neural v t , s t v_{t},s_{t} must be estimated stochastically at every step (e.g. via Hutchinson’s estimator), adding per-step cost and variance to the density updates rather than being a fundamental obstruction. For these reasons we do not compare against SuperDiff in our experiments. Adapting their density-tracking construction to bridge interpolants, either by re-deriving the AND weights so that equation 68 is closed by the choice of κ \kappa , or by initialising from a coupling under which the initial gap vanishes, is a natural future direction.

sections.heading: EMNIST to CMNIST.
sections.text: The source distribution ρ 0 \rho_{0} is the EMNIST dataset restricted to ten letter classes ( a-e , A-E ), the target distribution ρ 1 \rho_{1} is the Colored MNIST dataset with ten digit and ten colour classes (10 colours are multiplied by the greyscale MNIST samples). Images are rendered as 28 × 28 28{\times}28 RGB tensors in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Each sample is initialised from a concrete source image and transported toward CMNIST while enforcing a Boolean formula φ \varphi over Digit ( d ) (d) and Color ( c ) (c) atoms. We evaluate fixed templates (AND, OR ME , OR CI , AND ¬ \neg ) and randomly generated expression trees of depth two–three over the same atom vocabulary, while ensuring that conditional independence and mutual exclusivity hold. Cross-axis formulas such as Digit ( d ) ∨ Color ​ ( c ) (d)\lor\texttt{Color}(c) use the OR-CI rule of Section A.1 , while same-axis pairs such as Digit ( d 1 ) ∨ Digit ​ ( d 2 ) (d_{1})\lor\texttt{Digit}(d_{2}) (or the analogue for colours) use OR-ME.

sections.heading: CelebA.
sections.text: We train a stochastic interpolant from CelebA female to male images in the latent space of the FLUX.1-schnell VAE ( 16 16 channels, 16 × 16 16{\times}16 spatial resolution). Logical atoms are two binary CelebA attributes: Glasses and Hat . We test the logical statements AND, OR-CI, and AND ¬ \neg . Decoded outputs are evaluated at 128 × 128 128{\times}128 in pixel space.

sections.heading: QM9.
sections.text: We bridge noisy source molecules drawn from the QM9 dataset (matched in atom count to each target) to target molecules from QM9. Each graph carries 3 3 D coordinates and a 5 5 -way atom-type vector over { H , C , N , O , F } \{\mathrm{H},\mathrm{C},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{O},\mathrm{F}\} , coordinates are center-of-mass centred. Atoms are binary molecular attributes (ring presence, oxygen presence, etc.) composed with the same LogDiff rules as in Section 3.2 . The main logical statement pairs has_rings = 1 =1 with has_oxygen = 1 =1 under AND, OR-CI, and AND ¬ \neg . Bridge sources are restricted to molecules whose ground-truth labels violate the rule, so conformity measures whether the sampler can create the constraint from a non-conforming start.

sections.heading: Velocity and score fields.
sections.text: Both fields are U-Net-style ResNets with base width 96 96 , conditioning dimension 64 64 , and 3 3 -channel 28 × 28 28{\times}28 inputs. The encoder-decoder has three downsample stages (average pooling) and skip connections; residual blocks use FiLM-style modulation ( Perez et al., 2018 ) from the combined ( digit , colour , t ) (\text{digit},\text{colour},t) embedding. The velocity head outputs a 3 3 -channel field, the score head outputs a 3 3 -channel score and, on its bottleneck features, two auxiliary classifiers (digit and colour logits) used at sampling time.

sections.heading: Noise-aware classifier (guidance).
sections.text: During sampling, atom log-probabilities π ^ ​ ( c i ∣ x t ) \widehat{\pi}(c_{i}\mid x_{t}) for disjunction and negation are read from the score network’s auxiliary heads: the model is queried with the unconditional wildcard label on both axes, and log-softmax probabilities are taken for the atom’s digit or colour value at the current ( x t , t ) (x_{t},t) . No separate guidance classifier is trained for CMNIST.

sections.heading: Conformity evaluator.
sections.text: Rule conformity on generated images is measured with a held-out classifier: ResNet18 adapted for 28 × 28 28{\times}28 inputs ( 3 × 3 3{\times}3 stem, no initial max-pool) with separate linear heads for digit and colour. This model is trained only on clean Colored MNIST and is not used inside the sampler. Accuracy of the classifier is reported in Table 3 .

sections.heading: Velocity and score fields.
sections.text: Both fields are class-conditional SiT transformers trained on 16 × 16 16{\times}16 VAE latents with 16 16 input channels, patch size 1 1 , hidden size 384 384 , depth 12 12 , and 6 6 attention heads. CelebA’s 40 40 binary attributes are embedded with a multi-label encoder (per-attribute 3 3 -way tables: negative / positive / wildcard) and summed with a sinusoidal timestep embedding. Outputs are unpatchified to a 16 16 -channel velocity or score field in latent space.

sections.heading: Noise-aware classifier (guidance).
sections.text: OR and AND ¬ \neg require time-conditioned atom posteriors on the noisy latent x t x_{t} . We train a SiT model on the same latent geometry (patch size 2 2 , hidden size 192 192 , depth 6 6 , 6 6 heads) with timestep conditioning only. The model outputs 40 40 independent logits; at step t t the probability that attribute a a equals value v v is σ ⁡ ( ℓ a ) \sigma(\ell_{a}) if v = 1 v{=}1 and 1 − σ ⁡ ( ℓ a ) 1-\sigma(\ell_{a}) if v = 0 v{=}0 . With probability 0.1 0.1 during classifier training, t = 0 t{=}0 and clean latents are shown so the network is calibrated near the source endpoint.

sections.heading: Conformity evaluator.
sections.text: After VAE decoding to 128 × 128 128{\times}128 RGB, conformity uses a ResNet classifier trained on male CelebA samples with a 40 40 -way sigmoid head (as a training starting point the ResNet classifier was initialized with the ImageNet trained weights). Accuracy of the classifier is reported in Table 3 (Only the tested attributes are reported).

sections.heading: Velocity and score fields.
sections.text: Both fields are EGNNs built on fully connected molecular graphs (all ordered atom pairs within each molecule). We use the EDM-stabilised EGNN variant with hidden size 256 256 , depth 9 9 , and 5 5 atom-type channels. Node inputs are continuous one-hot atom vectors and 3 3 D coordinates; a conditioning module adds a sinusoidal time embedding plus embeddings for the binary graph labels ( has_rings = 1 =1 , has_oxygen = 1 =1 etc.), each with an extra “unknown” index for classifier-free guidance. The network predicts equivariant position velocities and invariant atom-type velocities; discrete types are recovered by argmax at the end of sampling.

sections.heading: Noise-aware classifier (guidance).
sections.text: The classifier shares the same graph construction but is a classification-only stack (hidden size 256 256 , depth 6 6 ): equivariant message-passing blocks, mean pooling over nodes, layer norm, and a linear head producing one logit per binary attribute. It is trained on noisy graphs ( x t , h t ) (x_{t},h_{t}) with the same bridge noise as the generator; atom posteriors for OR / AND ¬ \neg are sigmoids of the corresponding logits at the current t t .

sections.heading: Validity and conformity.
sections.text: Chemical validity and rule satisfaction are evaluated with RDKit (not with a learned classifier like in the image cases). Conformity is defined only on RDKit-valid molecules.

sections.heading: Rule conformity.
sections.text: For a batch with logical formula φ \varphi , conformity is the fraction of generated images whose evaluator predictions satisfy φ \varphi . On CMNIST and CelebA the evaluator is the ResNet18 classifier, see last section. This is distinct from the noise-aware classifiers used inside the sampler.

sections.heading: FID.
sections.text: We report Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) with Inception-v3 pool3 features ( 2048 2048 -dimensional, torchmetrics implementation, normalize=True ). Generated and reference images are bilinearly resized to 128 × 128 128{\times}128 and clamped to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] before feature extraction. For CMNIST, FID is computed per expression : for each φ \varphi in the evaluation schedule, the reference set is the subset of real Colored MNIST training images whose ground-truth digit and colour satisfy φ \varphi ; generated samples for that batch are compared to this expression-conditioned reference (up to min ⁡ ( 10,000 , | subset | ) \min(10{,}000,\lvert\text{subset}\rvert) real images). The reported FID is the mean across expression batches. For CelebA, it is similar. We report the FID scores with the expression-conditioned references (up to 5,000 5{,}000 reals).

sections.heading: RDKit validity.
sections.text: For each molecule we build an RDKit conformer from predicted coordinates and atomic numbers, infer bonds, and run SanitizeMol . The validity rate is the fraction of samples for which this pipeline succeeds.

sections.heading: Rule conformity.
sections.text: On valid molecules only, we recompute binary attributes from the perceived structure: ring-based labels via RDKit ring perception ( has_rings , etc.) and element-presence labels by atomic number. Conformity is the fraction of valid molecules whose recomputed attributes satisfy φ \varphi (AND / OR / AND ¬ \neg over the two chosen atoms).

sections.heading: Joint success.
sections.text: The primary success metric reported in the main figures is validity × conformity \text{validity}\times\text{conformity} (equivalently, the fraction of all samples that are both valid and rule-conforming).

sections.heading: Structural edit distance (RMSD).
sections.text: To calculate the distance between source and final molecule, we first apply the Kabsch algorithm ( Kabsch, 1976 ) after centering both structures at zero centre of mass, removing rigid rotation ambiguity, and second calculate the RMSD between the positions of the atoms. As a baseline, we calculate the mean Kabsch-RMSD between two random QM9 molecules. This is purely a geometric metric, the atomtypes are not taken into account.

sections.heading: Novelty.
sections.text: Valid molecules are converted to canonical SMILES. Novelty is the fraction of unique valid SMILES not present in a reference set of canonical SMILES for the full QM9 dataset.

sections.heading: B.4.3 Compute matching and error bars
sections.text: Network-evaluation (NFE) budgets for LoGSI vs. matched baselines follow Section 5 : outer steps N N with K K corrector substeps are matched against a K = 0 K{=}0 baseline with additional integration steps, such that the number of evaluations of the velocity and score networks match. When multiple training or evaluation seeds are run, main-text error bars aggregate across seeds for training and evaluation.

Mathias Niepert Affiliation: NEC Laboratories Europe Affiliation: University of Stuttgart Abstract Guidance and composition of generative models have applications in visual design, chemistry, and biology. Logical guidance composes conditional scores exactly for diffusion models. However, fm ( fm ) and si ( si ) learn velocity fields. We show that negation and exclusive disjunction admit exact conditional velocity composition on any interpolant, whereas conjunction, and therefore any formula containing one, is exact on Gaussian paths but in general incurs a drift-interaction error, so composed velocities need not sample the logical target. LoGSI solves this by using score-based re-equilibration as our principled mechanism and falling back to the Gaussian-path velocity rule as an approximate transport predictor. In non-Gaussian bridge problems, generation alternates transport steps with score re-equilibration steps. On image transfer (EMNIST to CMNIST, CelebA) and QM9 source-to-target molecular editing with logical attribute constraints, LoGSI improves rule conformity at the same network-evaluation budget over composed-velocity baselines, while also improving fidelity on the image tasks. More broadly, LoGSI applies wherever stochastic interpolants need guidance and logical combinations of constraints are natural. 1 Introduction Guidance and composition are central to generative AI, enabling controlled generation across domains ranging from visual design to chemistry and biology ( Saharia et al., 2022 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ; Watson et al., 2023 ; Skreta et al., 2025 ; Blohm and Garg, 2026 ) . Guidance steers a model toward desired properties, while composition combines multiple conditions or concepts to produce outputs that satisfy more complex requirements. Most existing methods target diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Song et al., 2020 ) , where one endpoint is a fixed Gaussian, and the reverse dynamics depend only on the score. A natural extension is to lift logical guidance to stochastic interpolants (SI) ( Albergo et al., 2025 ) , which unify diffusion and flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) and are not tied to a Gaussian endpoint. Classical guidance ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) for SI has been studied ( Feng et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) , but logical composition of atomic conditions in this regime remains open. We focus on domain transfer ( Liu et al., 2023 ) : an interpolant transports a source distribution ρ 0 ho_{0} to a target ρ 1 ho_{1} , samples can be initialized from concrete source instances ( Albergo et al., 2024 ) , and guidance enforces a Boolean formula φ \varphi over target attributes. For example, we may edit a source molecule by adding a geometry (e.g. rings) and an atom-composition constraint (e.g. oxygen). Throughout, we distinguish between unconditional velocity and score fields (or velocities and scores for short), denoted by v t ​ ( x ) v_{t}(x) and s t ​ ( x ) s_{t}(x) , and conditional velocity and score fields, denoted by v t ​ ( x ∣ c ) v_{t}(x\mid c) and s t ​ ( x ∣ c ) s_{t}(x\mid c) , which steer generation toward samples satisfying a constraint or property c c . The core challenge is that SIs learn conditional velocities, but it is not clear a priori how these fields should be combined to enforce a Boolean formula φ \varphi . For conditional scores, Alesiani et al. (2026) (LogDiff) derive exact recursive composition rules. We show that the analogous velocity composition is exact for Gaussian-path bridges, and that outside that regime it fails if the Boolean formula contains conjunctions or conditional-independent disjunctions (CI-disjunctions). We introduce LoGSI to address this asymmetry between velocity and score compositionality ( Figure 1 ). On general stochastic interpolants with a non-Gaussian starting distribution, both velocity and score are available at sampling time, but only the score admits exact logical composition for every formula ( Alesiani et al., 2026 ) . In LoGSI , composed velocities are exact on Gaussian-path bridges and can be used as a proxy transport field elsewhere. LoGSI therefore separates roles: an approximate transport step along the proxy transport field v ~ t ( ⋅ ∣ φ ) 	ilde{v}_{t}(\cdot\mid\varphi) advances mass along the interpolant, while exact composed conditional scores re-equilibrate samples toward p t ( ⋅ ∣ φ ) p_{t}(\cdot\mid\varphi) at each timestep. In the limit of sufficient score-correction steps at fixed t t , the procedure is consistent with the logical target. Concretely, we realize this split as a transport–re-equilibration sampler: each outer step applies a transport update along v ~ t 	ilde{v}_{t} , followed by K K overdamped Langevin steps with the exactly composed conditional score. We evaluate our method on image and molecular transfer with non-Gaussian endpoints, testing general Boolean templates (conjunction, disjunction, negation) and randomly generated expression trees. At matched network-evaluation budget, score-guided re-equilibration with a proxy velocity improves rule conformity over composed-velocity integration. It also yields higher fidelity on the image experiments. Figure 1: Overview of LoGSI . (a) Logical composition targets samples from ρ 1 ho_{1} satisfying c 1 ∧ c 2 c_{1}\land c_{2} , transported from ρ 0 ho_{0} by a stochastic interpolant, sampling can only use the atomic conditioned scores and velocities. (b) Scores compose exactly for general stochastic interpolants, velocity composition matches the same rule on Gaussian-path / diffusion bridges, except at negation and exclusive-disjunction nodes, which match on any interpolant ( Theorem 1 ). (c) Our method transports samples with a proxy velocity roughly pointing in the right direction, then re-equilibrates with the exactly composed conditional score. Our main contributions are as follows: • Score–velocity asymmetry for logical SI. On Gaussian-path flow matching, LogDiff score composition induces an exact velocity composition rule. For general stochastic interpolants with non-Gaussian endpoints, score composition carries over unchanged, velocity rules fail for conjunction and CI-disjunction, and therefore for general logical statements φ \varphi . • Logical guidance by score correction. We sample under Boolean formulas by re-equilibrating with exactly composed conditional scores at each timestep, avoiding any closed-form composed velocity field. • Proxy velocity transport. We reuse the Gaussian-path velocity rule as a transport proxy, cutting the number of correction steps needed and improving conformity over the composed-velocity baseline. 2 Related Work Generative methods and bridges. Diffusion models generate data by reversing a fixed noising process ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song and Ermon, 2020 ) , unified by Song et al. (2021) in the notion of stochastic processes. Song et al. (2021) also propose to sample with a predictor-corrector scheme, where a Langevin corrector uses the score to remove the predictor’s discretization error while both target the same marginal. Our sampler is similar but structurally different: because only the score composes exactly for formulas containing conjunctions or general disjunctions ( Remark 1 ), the score–velocity asymmetry ( Section 4.2 ) forces the transport step to be a deliberate proxy v ~ t ≠ v t ( ⋅ ∣ φ ) 	ilde{v}_{t}
eq v_{t}(\cdot\mid\varphi) , while the corrector is the exactness mechanism enforcing the logical constraint, needed beyond discretization error even with infinitesimal transport steps. Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) learns a velocity field between two distributions, and stochastic interpolants ( Albergo et al., 2025 ) generalize both diffusion and flow matching while dropping the Gaussian-endpoint assumption, which is why we adopt them for our method. Finally, Schrödinger bridges ( De Bortoli et al., 2021 ; Shi et al., 2023 ) transport between arbitrary distributions under an entropy-optimal-transport objective. Since our logical composition is orthogonal to how the bridge is trained, extending it to such samplers is an appealing direction for future work. Guidance and compositional conditioning. Guidance of generative models was first achieved by training a separate classifier to steer diffusion sampling ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) . The noise-aware classifiers we use for the posterior weights in our logical composition play an analogous role. Classifier-free guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) shortly after removed the need for a separately trained classifier by jointly modeling conditional and unconditional scores. Both approaches condition on a single condition and do not address how multiple conditions should be combined. Compositional generation, started in products of experts ( Hinton, 2002 ) and revived more recently ( Du et al., 2023 ; Gaudi et al., 2025 ) , targets exactly this problem, and subsequent work developed compositional and logical conditioning for diffusion models ( Liu et al., 2022 ) . Closely related, Skreta et al. (2025) introduce SuperDiff, which composes pretrained diffusion models at inference time through logical AND and OR operators. We discuss the connection to our bridge setting in Section A.6 . Most relevant to us, Alesiani et al. (2026) derive exact recursive rules for composing conditional scores under Boolean formulas.
